$comment: Published package versions, verified against the registry by CI on every run.
This file exists because consumers read the repository when they cannot query the
registry, and a repository tag is not a package version. Reading
packages/<name>/package.json at a tag reports the source tree at that moment, not what
is published; that has caused several repositories to report defects fixed releases
earlier. Rather than telling consumers not to read the repository, this file makes the
repository answer correctly, and scripts/check-published-versions.mjs fails CI if it
drifts from the registry.
Safe to read at a tag: the check runs on main, so any commit you can check out had this
file matching the registry at that time. Newer versions may exist; none of the versions
named here will be wrong.
MAINTAINERS: this file records what is PUBLISHED, so it cannot lead a publish. Do not
bump it in the same pull request that bumps packages/<name>/package.json -- the registry
check will fail the PR, correctly, because the version named here would not yet exist.
The order is: merge the code with this file untouched, push the tag so publish.yml runs,
then open a follow-up that updates this file to match. Between those two steps this file
is behind, which is the safe direction: every version named here still resolves.
Read "channels" below before reporting that you are blocked on package access. Three
separate repositories reported being blocked on all three packages, and this file told them
that only one was installed from the registry. THEY WERE RIGHT AND THIS FILE WAS WRONG.
tsconfig and prettier-config were recorded as channel "vendored" -- never published, no
token needed -- while all three packages are private: false and publish.yml publishes every
directory under packages/ unconditionally without consulting channel. All three have always
been on the registry. All three need a token. All three are gated on the same visibility
grant.
The evidence was in this repository's own CI on every run: check-published-versions prints
"versions.json matches the registry for 3 of 3 package(s)", which is only possible if all
three are published -- and that line was quoted as proof this file was correct. A check can
be passing, accurate, and read as confirming the opposite of what it says. Co-locating an
explanation with a value does nothing if nothing checks the value, so the legend is now
enforced: a channel claiming requiresRegistryAuth false must be backed by a package with
private: true, and a channel no package uses cannot stay in this file. Both are tested.
Copy "range" literally. Do not rewrite it as a caret. Every package here is below 1.0,
and for a 0.x version npm reads ^0.2.0 as >=0.2.0 <0.3.0 -- it pins the MINOR, not the
major. So ^0.2.0 silently refuses 0.12.0 and every fix in between. This has now bitten
eleven separate repositories: one adopted ^0.1.0, one planned ^0.2.0 while reporting a
React/ESLint 10 crash that had already been fixed, one re-pinned ^0.1.0 to ^0.2.0 and
believed it was current, one wrote ^0.2.0 for all three into a tracking issue kept
deliberately as a durable record, and one adopted prettier-config at ^0.2.0 and verified
it thoroughly -- resolved proseWrap, printWidth, parser, and a green format:check, all
true -- while 0.3.0 was published. That sixth case is the instructive one: a stale
version passes a behavioural test because it behaves correctly. What it lacks is absent
capability, not wrong behaviour, and no test written against the features you already
use can see one you have not used yet. The release its caret excluded was the one
widening prettier-plugin-svelte to v4, in a Svelte repository. Verify the resolved
version with npm ls; currency is a separate claim from correctness.
The seventh is the same repository as the fourth, on its FOURTH revision of the same
tracking issue, recording ^0.3.0 / ^0.3.0 / ^0.2.0 -- all three excluding the current
release, eslint-config by nine minors. Re-deriving a range four times and reaching a
caret every time is not carelessness; it is the notation being the default a hand
reaches for. That is why this file records an explicit upper bound and a test rejects
caret forms: the fix has to live in what gets copied, because the habit is not fixable
by being told. The eighth arrived from a DIFFERENT repository at the identical triple
^0.3.0 / ^0.3.0 / ^0.2.0, reached independently, as a deliberate CORRECTION off ^0.1.0
-- and it was announced with five green gates behind it, including a build, a full test
suite and a resolved TypeScript version checked against both peer ranges. Two repos
converging on the same wrong triple says the caret is not a slip but the shape the
notation pulls toward, and the green gates say again what the sixth case said: passing
checks measure behaviour, never currency.
The ninth closes the loop on the sixth and is the sharpest form of the trap: a THIRD
Svelte repository held prettier-config at ^0.2.0 deliberately while reporting, as an
open upstream defect, that its prettier-plugin-svelte peer of ^3.2.0 was stale against
the 4.1.1 they run. 0.3.0 -- the single release their own caret excludes -- is the one
that widened that peer to ^3.2.0 || ^4.0.0. The pin excluded the fix for the defect
being reported, so the bug report and its remedy were separated by the version range
alone. This is what makes the caret worse than an ordinary stale pin: it does not merely
withhold a fix, it makes the fix invisible, because the release that contains it is
never fetched and never read. A consumer can then rediscover, escalate and track a
defect that has already shipped -- three of them did, at real cost. In every case the
range recorded below was correct and
was rewritten into a caret out of habit. The failure is silent -- the install succeeds,
and you get an old package that behaves exactly as its bug reports describe. A test
rejects caret and tilde forms in this file so the recorded value stays safe to paste.
An earlier revision of the paragraph above said that crash was fixed in 0.8.0. It was
fixed in 0.4.0; 0.8.0 was merely the latest release when the sentence was written. That
number was wrong in the file that exists specifically to stop people reasoning from wrong
version numbers, and it was also quoted at a consumer to characterise a live defect report
as a stale read. Bisecting the published tarballs settled it in minutes and should have
been done before the claim, not after the report. Two lessons, both general: a fixed-in
version is a claim about the registry and has to be checked against it like any other, and
the latest release is not the release that fixed the thing -- writing it down as if it were
converts an ordinary approximation into a citation someone else will act on.
The tenth and eleventh are two more repositories at ^0.6.0, both reached after being given
a correct floor, and both measured carefully: one diffed the computed rule set across three
versions and found them byte-identical, the other across two. Both conclusions were true
and neither could see what the caret excluded, because a rule-set diff compares the
versions you fetched. That is the sixth case again in its most rigorous form: more
measurement does not escape the trap, because the trap is upstream of what gets measured.
Writing a range down somewhere durable does not make it correct, and a stale range in a
tracking issue outlives the chat that would have corrected it. If you record these
values outside your repository, record the URL of this file next to them.
Do not write a npm specifier for a vendored package at all. All three packages below are
channel "registry" today, so this does not currently apply to any of them -- it is kept
because a consumer listed all three as dependencies, was told two were vendored and
unblocked, and lost time acting on advice this file was the source of.

registry.summary: Installed from GitHub Packages. Requires a token.
notes: Add it to package.json and install it. GitHub Packages authenticates every read,
including reads of a public package, so contributors and CI both need a classic PAT
with read:packages. Package visibility affects authorization, not authentication.
